#4090. After a year of testing, one of Steam's best features is finally out of beta, making it easier to find games you might actually like

Steam's Personal Calendar, a feature Valve has been testing for nearly a year, has finally left beta and is now available for everyone.

Personal Calendar, which initially launched as a Steam Labs experiment last October, works by highlighting upcoming games and recent releases - tailored to your interests - and arranging them by release date. The feature has its own section on the store homepage, and also has a dedicated page showing the games Steam's algorithm believes you're going to like, meaning what's included is different for everyone.

While Steam has always had several ways of recommending games to players based on their tastes, Personal Calendar takes it a step further by having a stricter recommendation criteria and arranging the results in an intuitive, month-based way that's less likely to overwhelm.

Valve says its recommendation engine relies on three key metrics: it looks at your recently played games, finds other players with similar playtime profiles, then looks at the games those players have been playing or adding to their wishlists. In a blog post, Valve explains only games "you play the most" are considered, meaning titles you try for a few minutes won't factor into your recommendations.

Crucially, the Personal Calendar's recommendations are not static, and Valve notes they're refreshed daily to incorporate new data where available. "In reality you aren't likely to see your recommendations change all that much from day to day," it writes, "but as time goes by you will obviously see new things pop up as the eight-week horizon of the calendar marches forward, or as games lock in their release dates."

Incidentally, Valve is aware the feature could end up having the opposite effect, i.e., limiting the number of games a player potentially sees because they fall outside their filters, essentially trapping them inside a bubble. The developer doesn't have a clear solution for that potential problem, but says it wants to keep things varied.

"With the Personal Calendar, it's unlikely that every day has a new game launching that is the same genre/theme as games you've been playing and is also a good recommendation for you," Valve explains. "As a result, the recommendations generated by the Personal Calendar end up drawing from a wider pool of titles across all kinds of genres that are releasing each day."

#4089. Guide: Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Walkthrough (Switch 2 Remake): Guide To The Main Quest, Side Quests & Collectables

Zelda: Ocarina of Time is a dense adventure with many secrets to find, and while the critical path is fairly linear, it's rarely straightforward - asking you to pick up select items and upgrades before you can start exploring its many dungeons.

That's why a Zelda: Ocarina of Time walkthrough comes in handy. Though the Switch 2 version follows the same beats as the N64 original, we'd estimate around 10% of the game's puzzles and locations have been changed or updated - just enough to throw off those very familiar with the 1998 version.

This page features both an abridged and thorough walkthrough though the critical path, plus a repository of our other Zelda: Ocarina of Time guides, from optional side-quests to items and collectables.

On this page: Zelda: Ocarina Of Time Walkthrough (Switch 2 Remake): Guide To The Main Quest, Side Quests & Collectables

If you want brief directions and as few spoilers as possible in terms of item unlocks and progression, then use the following abridged walkthrough to take you through the game. If you want extra specifics - including useful optional extras as you go - then check the following section.

For a more detailed walkthrough of the critical path, this section can explain specific steps on how to progress. If you even more detailed step-by-step guides to the game's many dungeons, then follow the links to dedicated pages on each.

Before you can visit the Great Deku Tree, you must find a Sword and Shield, otherwise Mido won’t let you through. You can find the Kokori Sword in the Forest Training Center to the south-west (crawl through the vent to get there, then find it in the chest above), and the Deku Shield from the shop in the north-east by collecting Rupees found scattered around the village.

Visit the Deku Tree, complete the Great Deku Tree dungeon, and get the Kokiri’s Emerald key item and an instruction to head to Hyrule Castle. Now leave Kokiri Forest to the west to receive an Ocarina in a cutscene before leaving to Hyrule Field.

Head directly north along the path until you reach the castle drawbridge. The area inside is the Market - there’s lots of optional activities here, and when ready, proceed to Hyrule Castle, where after getting the Weird Egg from Maron, you must make your way through the grounds to meet Zelda.

You'll now have Zelda’s Letter and learnt Zelda’s Lullaby on the Ocarina. The critical path is to Death Mountain via Kakariko Village, though you should visit the Lost Woods first (for Saria's Song, which you'll need shortly) and ideally, an optional visit to Lon Lon Ranch (for a Bottle and the first step in how to get Epona).

When ready, go east from Hyrule Field’s drawbridge and up the steps to Kakariko Village.

After finding all Cucco locations for a Bottle and visiting the Graveyard for the Sun’s Song (both optional), show Zelda’s Letter to the guard at the north exit. He gives you an optional errand - returning to the Hyrule Castle Market for a "proper shield" (the Hylian Shield) and also to start the Happy Mask Shop quest.

The aim is to reach Goron City. Hug the right most wall: this will take you up and round the corner, then back on yourself up the cliff. The path will now split: take the left branch to Goron City.

Inside Goron City, head to the lowest level, where at the north side is a closest door. Play Zelda’s Lullaby here to open it. Inside is Darunia. Talk to him, then play Saria’s Song (which you can get from the Lost Woods). This will see you unlock the Goron’s Bracelet, allowing you to use Bomb Flowers.

Now leave Goron City the way you came (the top entrance), then go directly right to see a Bomb Flower near a fence. Now you have the Goron's Bracelet, throw it over and you’ll bomb the entrance to Dodongo Cavern, allowing you to enter.

Once you have completed the Dodongo Cavern dungeon and picked Bombs and the Goron’s Ruby (the Spiritual Stone of Fire), feel free to scale Death Mountain for a Great Fairy location (unlocking Din's Fire) before heading off to Zora Domain.

Zora River - which leads to Zora Domain - is just east of Kakariko Village and Death Mountain on Hyrule Field.

Reach the end - the way there is fairly linear - and access Zora Domain by playing Zelda's Lullaby at the waterfall.

Inside, you must find the whereabouts of Princess Ruto by getting the Silver Scale in a mini-game at the top of the waterfall, then by visiting Lake Hylia via the underwater shortcut for a Bottle with a letter inside. (Our dedicated Zora Domain walkthrough features more specific directions for all these, by the way!)

Speak to King Zora, Bottle up a fish found in Zora Domain, then give it to the giant fish in Zora Fountain to access Lord Jabu-Jabu's Belly dungeon.

Once the dungeon is complete and the Spiritual Stone of Water is in your possession, head to Hyrule Castle. After the cutscene, dive in the moat and collect the Ocarina of Time, where you’ll then learn the Song of Time.

Head to the Temple of Time which branches off from Hyrule Castle Market. Inside, stand in front of the inscription at the far end, and play the Song of Time. Now go into the next room and retrieve the Master Sword.

After the cutscene, you’ll become Adult Link, and are told to head to Kakariko Village. Do so, then head to the Graveyard. On the left row of graves is a tombstone with flowers in front; push the stone and head down the hole. Now follow Dampe through the maze and at the end, you’ll receive the Hookshot.

To leave, play the Song of Time on the blocks, to emerge out in the Windmill. Use this opportunity to get the Heart Piece opposite, then speak to the man to learn the Song of Storms - you’ll need this later.

With the Hookshot in hand, you can explore more of Hyrule, but when ready, head to Forest Temple: it can be found at the end of the Lost Woods, and inside the dungeon, you'll unlock the Bow and be rewarded with the Forest Medallion story item.

Complete the Forest Temple dungeon to unlock a Sage. At this point onward, upon returning to the Temple of Time, you can time travel back into Young Link by putting the Master Sword the pedestal. Also, to help, Sheik will teach you The Prelude of Light, which allows you to teleport back to the Temple of Time - a pretty handy shortcut.

As Adult Link, make your way to Death Mountain (it’s worth going into the Shooting Gallery in Kakariko Village now you have the Bow, which rewards you the Big Quiver to hold 40 Rupees as you go) then head into Goron City.

On the next level down is a Goron rolling around, and your aim is to detonate a Bomb near him so he stops. Once successful, the Goron will reveal their name is Link, son of Darunia, and will explain the Goron's plight.

Exhaust the dialogue options to receive the Goron Tunic - a red garb which allows you to withstand high temperatures - and directions to the Fire Temple, which is by heading to Darunia’s room (located on the bottom level at the back) and then by pulling the statue to reveal a route to the Death Mountain Crater.

Once in, go over the drawbridge using the Hookshot to meet Sheik, who will teach you Bolero of Fire. Now head through the left doorway, drop down and follow the passage to reach the dungeon, unlocking the Megaton Hammer and the Fire Medallion along the way.

Head to the Ice Cavern, which is located in Zora Domain (or specifically, in Zora Fountain where you encountered Lord Jabu-Jabu as a child). Doing so will see you unlock the Iron Boots; make sure you grab a Blue Fire before leaving, and return to Zora Domain and use the Blue Fire on King Zora to free him and receive a Blue Tunic, which allows you to breathe underwater for an unlimited amount of time.

With both the Iron Boots and Blue Tunic in hand, we have everything we need to take on the Water Temple. Play the Serenade of Water to be teleported there when ready. Completing this will see you receive the Longshot - a Hookshot upgrade - and the Water Medallion.

Before we move onto the next temple, on this island is a plaque in front of you which hints at a puzzle involving the morning sun. If you are reading this as soon as the Water Temple has wrapped, the sun should still be rising: aim for the halo with your Bow and fire an Arrow, which will see it transform into a Fire Arrow on the platform ahead.

When you’re ready, head to Kakariko Village as Adult Link. When you arrive, a cutscene plays showing the place on fire, Sheik appearing, and a spirit emerges from the well. You’re then taught the Nocturne of Shadow, allowing you to travel to the Shadow Temple - though there’s a place to visit you need to visit first - the Kakariko well.

As it's currently blocked off as an adult, so you need to return as a child. If you haven’t already, learn Song of Storms from the Guru-Guru inside the windmill, then return to the windmill as Young Link and play Song of Storms back to him (now you have the Nocturne of Shadow, the return journey will be a lot quicker).

Doing so will cause the windmill to spin out of control and lower the water in the well. Drop down and complete the Bottom of the Well mini-dungeon to get the Lens of Truth.

If you haven’t already, you also need Din’s Fire. This is acquired by visiting the Great Fairy location at the top of Death Mountain. Now you have Din’s Fire and the Lens of Truth, play Nocturne of Shadow, then use Din’s Fire in the centre of the torches to gain access to the Shadow Temple, where you’ll get the Hover Boots along the way, and another Medallion.

With that done, it’s time to head to Gerudo Valley. It’s found in the west of Hyrule Field, and you need either the Longshot or Epona to make it over the bridge at the start.

Complete the Gerudo’s Fortress stealth section - essentially let yourself get captured, then find the four carpenters so you can explore freely - then make your way across the Mirage Desert's trials (you need the Longshot and the Lens of Truth) to reach the Evil Desert Colossus area and the Spirit Temple. This unlocks two new items - the Silver Gauntlets and the Mirror Shield - and another Medallion.

The Gerudo Valley area also features two optional extras - another Great Fairy spell (Bomb the wall on the north wall of the Evil Desert Colossus) and within Gerudo’s Fortress, the Gerudo Training Ground (a mini-dungeon which grants the Ice Arrow.

Assuming you have now awakened every Sage and received every Medallion, it’s now time to head to the Temple of Time and start the final stretch of the game.

A cutscene will play and you’ll receive the Light Arrow, and an instruction to head to Ganon’s Castle.

Approach the lava moat around the castle to form a bridge with the help of the Sages. The dungeon within is composed of six ‘routes’ from a central hub; though you can tackle them in broadly any order, go for the Shadow Barrier to unlock the Golden Gauntlets first, which is required for completing every puzzle.

Once that - and a brief trip to the Great Fairy just outside the castle beyond the bridge for a useful defensive upgrade - it’s time to scale the tower, or to halt your progress so you can mop up any remaining side-quests and collectables (see the end of this guide for a list) before the finale.

The tower within Ganondorf’s Castle is essentially a short gauntlet of battles until you reach Ganon himself at the top, and from there, it’s a linear stretch until the end credits. Good luck!

Here is a list of side quests, items and collectables you can find. Note this is in-progress, and will become more comprehensive in the days following launch:

Matthew - an award-winning UK-based writer and editor specialising in guides and service articles - joined the Nintendo Life team in May 2026.

#4088. Monarchs at Play is a 4X strategy city-builder about chaining hexagonal tiles that only takes an hour out of your day

None of us have any bloody time any more, do we? The economy being in the toilet is obviously part of that, but the other part is that we're all adults and now we have to do responsible adult things like our laundry, and buying toilet paper, and buying toilet paper again because it simply never ends. It all makes playing games just that little bit trickier, especially when it comes to lengthy strategy game runs. If you're longing for a quick dose of some 4X strategy, though, Monarchs at Play, a turn-based city-builder that only takes an hour, might be the thing you're after.

I know that a simple hour of your time might actually be quite a lot in the greater scheme of things, but for something like a 4X strategy game, that sounds pretty reasonable to me. In Monarchs at Play, you choose from one of several monarchs, each of which has their own unique abilities and buildings. In a run, like most other city-builders, you start out small by placing what little buildings you have available to you, the ultimate goal being to place different kinds of tiles next to one another to build up combos.

Different buildings allow you to rack up resources, which in turn lets you place new buildings; you get how this works! You aren't doing this alone, however, as you have rivals to compete against, where you'll have to destroy the buildings they place to continue growing your own empire. These rivals can just be simple NPCs, but they can also be real-life players, so if you've only got an hour to spare but want to play something online, Monarchs at Play seems like it'll be a good fit.

There's a demo you can currently check out and try for yourself on Steam too. No release date attached just yet, so you'll have to keep your eyes peeled.

#4087. As beloved Dishonored studio faces closure, Xbox agrees union request to extend negotiations deadline in hope of saving 217 jobs

Xbox has extended Arkane Lyon's consultation period by around a month, as the search for a new owner continues. If one isn't found, the studio will likely be shut down.

Arkane Lyon - the developer behind immersive sims including Dishonored and Deathloop - was one of several first-party studios impacted by Xbox CEO Asha Sharma's sweeping "reset", which will result in 3,200 job losses by the time the process is complete. Arkane's leadership was reportedly informed of Xbox's intention to close the studio on 16th July, but France's Florange Law meant a three-month search for a buyer must first be undertaken.

Last week, unions - Printemps Écologique and Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo - were said to be fighting to buy more time for negotiations. And now, as per a new report by Le Monde, Microsoft has agreed to extend the original 13th November deadline to December. If a buyer still isn't found, 217 jobs are at risk.

Documents published on the French government's website in August referenced a plan for "the complete and permanent cessation of the company's activities" and another for the "dismissal of all employees for economic reasons."

A Microsoft representative confirmed the deadline extension to PC Gamer, telling the outlet: "We have extended the consultation period by one additional month as we explore options, including finding a partner to support the studio through the development work still ahead." That "development work" refers to Marvel's Blade, which seems to still be under Arkane's purview even now.

"This is a defined extension, and we remain committed to keeping the Works Council informed throughout the process," Microsoft added. As for the filings referring to the closure of Arkane and the redundancy of its developers, the company spokesperson said they are a "part of the required consultation process and do not represent a final decision."

According to members of Printemps Ecologique (thanks VGC), Marvel's Blade is almost complete. The union says it would be a "monumental waste" for the game not to be released. However, a PC Gamer source also claimed Marvel's Blade - which has remained something of an enigma since its unveiling back in 2023 - still has years to go until it is finished.

Arkane's possible closure as part of Xbox's massive wave of cuts has already resulted in over 1,600 layoffs as restructuring continues. Sharma's "reset" has also included the jettisoning of beloved Psychonauts developer Double Fine, sweeping job cuts at Halo Studios as it transitions into a support studio, and job losses across various other Xbox-owned studios.

What's more, it seems Microsoft is far from done. According to a recent report, Xbox is planning three more waves of cuts:one this month, another in November, and a third in January.

#4086. Part idle game, part automation game, Moon Sweepers exploits the sickness in me that adores both Satisfactory and Cookie Clicker

In space, no one can hear you have an existential crisis

When Edwin talked about Moon Sweepers yesterday he focused on the artisanal approach to space rock cleaning. Like the puritan he is, he wants to wipe away all the dust on the moon using a toothbrush. He says you should take pride in your work, stick one spacesuit-clad middle finger up to the machines and say 'Fuck off, robots. Let me show you my art!" as you get down on all fours and brush away moon dust.

I mean, sure, when I first created a new game in Moon Sweepers, I painted with my toothbrush:

But then I got down to the serious business of trying to clean up the dusty moon, section by section and all thoughts of art left my head.

When you first begin Moon Sweepers, you're faced with an entire planetoid broken down into hexagonal tiles, each deep with dust and needing a brushing. The first sectors you'll clean take an age to clear. The toothbrush only carves a thin groove into the dirt and the tile is comparatively vast. Your backpack fills with hoovered up dust as you clean and when it's filled you need to head back to base to sell it off. Each kilo sold nets you a single dollar, but with that cash you can buy improved tools, swapping your toothbrush for a hand brush, and eventually for a broom.

It was only after I bought my broom I realised – too late to save myself – that I was playing an incremental game.

Moon Sweepers is an incremental game. There are sectors of dusty moon as far as the eye can see. The tools you start with a small, but they grow in potency, with increasingly large brooms that can be upgraded with wider brush heads and larger backpacks, meaning you can collect moon matter for longer before heading back to base to cash it in. But Moon Sweepers is also an automation game, and it's only when I clocked that that I realised I was truly done for.

Once you buy a hammer from your base's shop, you can start building conveyor belts, space dust processing plants, and robot vacuums. Stretch a conveyor out from your base to one of the sectors of the moon you're clearing and you can dump filled dust canisters on the belt instead of heading home to sell it. The conveyor whisks away the dust-filled tube and sells it for you, letting you spend longer in the fields scrubbing. Pour dust into a processing plant and it will compact it into a more valuable resource, earning you extra cash for your labour. And, well, robot vacuum cleaners look like NASA-branded Roombas. They clear the dust from a wide grid around their docking station.

Moon Sweepers, this incremental game in Satisfactory's clothing, now has me thinking I can genuinely clean the entire moon. I've abandoned Edwin's artful approach to the task and I am all in on using the robots, conveyor belts, and moon rovers to complete the job. I somehow believe this even though I have only so far cleaned 19 sectors and, according to the handbook, there are 163,842 in total. I believe this despite Steam reviews from players with many more hours under their belts shouting to me that this is a futile task. "We are 10 hours in and we are already maxed out on all the latest tools and vehicles and we are not even 1% done with cleaning," writes Marten. "20 hours played, just reached 1% of surface cleared," says Bim Fimberdim. "After 26 Hours I cleared 1.6% of the moon," writes Amigos_Of_Bako.

Maybe it's the ease and definition of progress, which is so unlike life. The irony of getting this fixated on Moon Sweepers is that I'm currently doing a lot of DIY in my flat and, despite resembling the manual labour in some of these games, it has none of the simplicity.

I went into this past weekend meaning to end it with a painted living room with some new alive bookshelves. I had to measure the alcove for some shelves, drill the holes for the brackets, cut the shelves to size, clean everything up, and then paint the living room. Yet, at the end of the weekend, I had fewer shelves and less paint on the walls than when I started. Delay after delay, complication after complication, and setback after setback meant that progress was slow and, when it did game, was more like a ship tacking against the wind than a straight line. What could have been a fulfilling, satisfying task, was infuriating and stressful.

Perhaps, right now, I want to clean up the moon because sweeping all of its 163,842 sections somehow feels more attainable and realistic than fitting these bookshelves.

#4085. First Phantom Blade Zero PS5 Update Makes an Early, Deadly Boss Easier

Hua, Deadly Betrothed nerfed in PS5 patch

S-GAME has today published the first major Phantom Blade Zero update for PS5 and PC, available to download now on both platforms.

It's a relatively normal list of updates and tweaks, comprising bug fixes and adjustments — until you see that one of the game's earlier bosses has been nerfed a touch. Hua, Deadly Bethrothed, an optional boss fight in the first main Weeping Creek Valley region, has had her grab attacks made less frequent.

This update applies the nerf to the Wayfarer (easy) and Pathbreaker (normal) difficulty options. If you are on Hellwalker (hard) or the 66 Days modes, then Hua will operate as she did before.

Once you reach the Sha-Chi Tower in Weeping Creek Valley, you access the boss arena by dropping down through a hole on the ground floor of the tower. From there, you round the corner and discover Hua. Her grab attack deals very heavy damage to Soul, but now that attack will be less frequent.

I think Hua is more designed as a boss encounter you return to later on in the campaign, once you're a bit stronger and have access to better, upgraded weapons and medicines. If you face her as soon as she's accessible, then the fight is doable, but it presents a big challenge.

Elsewhere, update 1.3 on PS5 adds new audio settings to the pause menu: Hit Sound Intensity and Hit Impact Sound Intensity.

You can then expect "improved performance" in certain areas, different combat behaviour for select enemies and bosses, and improved weapon feedback. Below you'll find all the patch notes for PS5 update 1.3.

#4083. Switch 2 Surpasses 26 Million Units Sold, Hardware Sales Down By 37.4%

Nintendo has released its latest financial report, confirming that the Switch 2 has now sold over 26 million units since its launch last year.

Coming in at more accurate 26.35 million, unit sales for the first half of the current fiscal year totalled 6.49 million. This represents a year-on-year decrease of 37.4%, with the company shifting 10.36 million during the same period last year.

Don't fret, though! This is to be expected. Console sales for the Switch 2 were astronomical during its first year on sale, so a decrease during its second year isn't going to come as a surprise. Couple in the hardware price hikes earlier this year, and it's clear that momentum has taken an expected downward turn.

Still, 26 million though folks. 26. Million. It's creeping up on the N64's lifetime sales at 32.93 million.

Software performed much better. Nintendo shifted a total of 24.49 million Switch 2 games over the first half of the year, an uptick of 18.8% over the same period last year. Similarly, Switch 1 software sold 65.72 million, an increase of 6.8&%. Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream and Rhythm Heaven Groove helped Nintendo achieve this, selling 8.81 million and 2.89 million respectively.

Nintendo's forecast for the fiscal year ending March 2027 remains unchanged at this time, so it's currently expecting to sell a total of 16.5 million Switch 2 units during the period.

#4082. Leaked Mass Effect 5 trailer is being "re-scored" by one of the original trilogy's composers, so folks can get a taste of his musical vision for the game

One of the composers who contributed to the scores of the original Mass Effect trilogy has decided to re-soundtrack the Mass Effect Universe trailer which leaked following the game's cancellation and BioWare's closure. Sam Hulick's aim, aside from making this year's N7 Day a tiny bit less depressing if he can deliver as planned, is to share some of his "musical vision" for the RPG.

Hulick announced his plan on BlueSky, having already started working on a new score for the trailer "for no reason other than closure". "My plan is to release the re-scored Mass Effect Universe trailer for N7 Day," he wrote. "A little tight, since I'm a bit busy pitching for a new game, but I'll see what I can do! I don't wanna rush it, and I want it to properly represent my musical vision for MEU."

With composer Austin Wintory having recently released a collection of tunes he put together while in talks to potentially work on a proper soundtrack for what would have been the fifth Mass Effect game, Hulick's efforts will mean there are two different takes on what Universe might've sounded like out there in the wild. It's somewhat of a silver lining to the dark cloud of the game's demise. You can rightly argue that any canned game tends to be eulogised in terms that point to it having had the potential to be the best thing since sliced bread in a fashion that perhaps over-eggs the pudding a bit, but it's always interesting to learn what those who did or could have worked on such games had in mind.

Having takes on Universe's soundtrack from both Hulick and Wintory out there certainly isn't hurting anyone. The former's also offered his view on the ongoing community-driven efforts to pressure EA into not putting the series on ice, as they have the likes of Burnout in the past. "What really sucks & cannot be undone is all the folks at BioWare who lost their jobs," he wrote. "Even if EA licensed the IP, that doesn't solve anything for them. Someone with a lotta cash would have to license it AND hire the team."

Pending that sort of miracle, the likes of the trailer, these tunes, and other details ex-BioWare devs have shared about what the studio hoped to achieve with Universe are at least meaning fans aren't entirely left in the dark about the work going on during BioWare's final chapter.

#4081. Control loreheads shouldn't put too much stock into what The Board says in Control Resonant - the devs say it's "basically gibberish"

One of Control and Control Resonant's most memorable stylistic choices is how The Board - an alien entity whose true nature is a mystery, and whose morals and motivations are never made clear - communicates with the player.

Clearly, developer Remedy knew exactly how The Board should sound coming out of your speakers. While there's no consensus, many have theories about what The Board is truly saying - and that's in part because of the way it sounds.

Except, it turns out what you hear shouldn't be taken very seriously.

"An important part of the design is that The Board is basically gibberish, not affiliated to any language," Control Resonant audio lead Lucas Pierrot told Gamespot. "So, when you hear a word, you tend to hear what you want to hear… and that's pretty neat in terms of audio design, as players can fulfill their fantasies."

The Board speaks an oblique language and in a very bassy voice, making it hard to make out what's being said from voice alone. The games' subtitles offer what could only be considered an interpretation of some of what's being said, but they alternate between different words for similar concepts to make it even harder for The Board's speech to have a definitive meaning.

Pierrot added, "You want to hear The Board praising you for performing an Execution? You can! Maybe you hear them saying 'Absolute cinema, Combo!' etc., but if you prefer to think they're arrogant and only feel disdain for slaying a weak enemy… you can hear that too!"

The Board's distinct way of communicating with the player was designed to run a gamut of emotions; Remedy wanted it to feel "scary, unsettling, or even funny sometimes". Pierrot also revealed a trick the audio team used to emphasise certain words, by adding a "pulse" sound and "low, soft kick" to them.

"I used this to give weight when necessary to have a nice flow. You can see it as some sort of trick to articulate sentences. It gives rhythm and punctuation," he explained.

Control Resonant has seemingly done well for Remedy, reaching 1m sales faster than any other game in studio history despite releasing in a very busy period. If you're looking to play it soon, Eurogamer's Control Resonant walkthrough is worth bookmarking to help you make good upgrade decisions and pick which activities to prioritise.

#4080. "Creation without a creator": Pathologic 3's devs have refused to patch an invisible apple tree, and for a blissful moment, I thought they were lying to poison Google's AI

"Maybe this apple tree is trying to tell us something."

Magnificent, depressing plague colony fable Pathologic 3 has received a sizeable game update that adds some new difficulty modes, a photo feature, and some new, worryingly folkloric methods of defeating a murky embodiment of disease. Developers Ice Pick Lodge have also staunchly refused to remove an invisible apple tree, describing this apparently "famous" bug as a hallmark of a game whose "symbolic nature has almost overtaken its function as a product". This appears to be the last major update for Pathologic 3, so that invisible apple tree is staying in the game forever.

I confess, when I first read the Steam blog in question, I doubted. The thing about invisible apple trees is that they are quite easy to confuse with apple trees that are simply not there. Pathologic in general is a house of lies: as Quintin Smith (RPS in peace) put it in his legendary Butchering Pathologic trilogy, "absolutely everybody has an angle, everyone's bending the truth and trying to twist you round their fingers." Pathologic 3 especially is a purgatorial time travel story that must be continually rewritten, a crock of festering rumours enclosed by an enormous, phantom theatre. As such, I read Ice-Pick's typically professorial account of the "invisible apple tree" with intense suspicion.

"Roger Ebert, the famous film critic, once argued that video games could never be art," the devs write on Steam. "It's curious, then, that urinals and bottle racks achieved that status with hardly any struggle, thanks to Marcel Duchamp. So Myst, StarCraft, or Pathologic can't be art, but a urinal can? The distinction, perhaps, lies in function. A urinal placed in a museum stops being plumbing and becomes a symbol. A video game, on the other hand, remains a functional object. We still have to use it.

"But enough about urinals," they go on. "Let's turn to another famous work: Joseph Kosuth's One and Three Chairs. In this work, a chair is no longer simply something to sit on. Whether it's comfortable hardly matters: as a work of art, it still functions. A video game can also become a symbolic chair. But you still have to sit on it. There's a running joke that Pathologic is a great game that nobody actually plays. Somehow, it really has become something like Kosuth's symbolic chair, one nobody is obliged to sit on. Which raises a question: should we even fix Pathologic if its symbolic nature has almost overtaken its function as a product?

"Take visual bugs, for instance. Are they broken chairs you can't sit on, or artistic decisions?" Ice-Pick continue. "Consider our famous invisible apple tree. Oh, apple tree! Why are you here? What are we supposed to do with you? This is probably the most famous bug in Pathologic 3. We've received more complaints about it than almost anything else. We have to admit there were moments when we genuinely hated that tree. Are we going to fix it in this update? Perhaps not.

"After all, it's a creation of the machine," they conclude. "Somehow, the game's code produced this impossible object. And over time, our annoyance at it has begun to turn into a strange affection. Sometimes an artistic act lies not in creating something, but in the artist's decision about it. Maybe this apple tree is trying to tell us something. So the tree stays."

Aside from making me pine for a world in which, say, EA add a "hypernormalisation" slider to The Sims, or Ubisoft redefine Assassin's Creed parkour as a Situationist dérive (yes, I too have read books), the blog post filled me with confusion. I couldn't remember any invisible apple trees in Pathologic 3. I also couldn't find any English language mention of Pathologic 3's avowedly "famous" ethereal vegetation on Google or the Steam forums, save for in stories covering the game's latest update.

My weakness for talk of symbolism notwithstanding, I began to worry that Ice-Pick might be winding us up. And by "us", I specifically mean pathetic videogame reporters, hunting for a cool bug anecdote to wrap a headline around. Pathetic videogame reporters who are subject to the wiles of Google Search, which has recently become an AI-driven abomination that subsumes and rewords all knowledge while starving actual information sources of traffic.

There have been efforts to screw with Google's AI summaries, planting nonsense on Reddit and elsewhere in the hope of skewing or outright sabotaging the chatbot's datasets. Perhaps Pathologic 3's "invisible apple tree" was one such poison apple, I mused to myself, offered to Gemini in the manner of a cackling forest hag thrusting suspiciously plump and juicy fruit at cherubic village children. Associations foamed in my brain: Ice-Pick Lodge are based in Kazakhstan... where apples first grew in the wild. Breathless, I contacted Ice-Pick Lodge for a clarification, and – bah, it turns out there is an invisible apple tree in Pathologic 3, after all.

"The slightly longer story goes like this," producer Alexander Souslov told me over DM. "At some point (nobody remembers exactly when), one of our tree assets - an apple tree, to be precise - started rendering incorrectly and became invisible. The leaves were still there, but the trunk was gone. We tried to fix it, but ran into the classic game developer's dilemma: is this really important enough to spend resources on, rather than, say, making another cutscene or putting together another quest?"

Souslov says the apple tree drove him "absolutely nuts". (I feel like he could have rolled with some line about "one bad apple spoiling the barrel", but hey, I'm not one of those stuffed shirts over at Edge Magazine - I don't mind interviewees mixing their arboreal metaphors.) Eventually, however, he made peace with the exasperatingly trunkless tree. "I started thinking: wait a minute, this thing basically came into existence all by itself. Do I really have to fix it?

"And that's when I remembered Marcel Duchamp and his ideas, and suddenly I began to feel that we'd accidentally created something beautiful," Souslov went on. "Invisible trees next to the Cathedral, where time flows in different directions. There's a strange kind of beauty in that, in the very act of creation without a creator.

"So I made an executive artistic decision: we're keeping the tree, and we're officially declaring it part of the world. So no pranks involved! Just a happy accident elevated to the status of artistic intent."

With Souslov's guidance, I fired up an old Pathologic 3 save and tracked down the invisible apple tree in-game, right next to the aforesaid Cathedral. Please find a picture of the thing's spectral foliage below – poetically captured by moonlight at the dead of 1am, through a fog of in-game Apathy. I also belatedly checked Reddit, and yep, there's a paper trail, though Souslov added that the bug is inconsistent: "their whimsical behavior makes it even better as an artistic expression - the apple tree may decide it won't meet with you today."

I remain compelled by the idea of developers telling dirty great porkies in their patchnotes, if only to excite and upset games journalists who really don't have this much time to spare. Mojang used to do that thing with Herobrine, remember?

Given the escalating chatbotification of everything, I think we are entering an exhilarating new age of lying on the internet, in which deceit and doublespeak have become weapons of resistance against the algorithm. But I also just think videogames and their creators are often more fun when they are two-faced, providing there's some fundamental benevolence involved. Videogames are all about sleight of hand, and devs should take more pleasure in that. Thank you to Pathologic 3 for planting this seed.

#4079. This JRPG Series Lightly Inspired by the Console Wars Is Finally Getting a New PS5 Sequel

Hyperdimension Neptunia intrigued me when it first released on the PS3, because its cast of characters were loosely inspired by the various console platforms, like PlayStation, Xbox, and (at the time) Wii.

The series gained a cult following and spawned dozens of sequels, spin-offs, and re-releases. But there hasn’t been a new mainline entry since 2015.

That changes in 2027 with the release of Hyperspace Neptunia: Unlimited on the PS5 and PS4, a full-blown sequel which first debuted in Japan earlier this year.

This version promises the most “expansive” magical girl action ever, with new mechanics and deeper dungeons.

“A whole new adventure has opened up for the Goddesses where dungeons are more expansive than ever. Goddesses can seamlessly switch from running to flight to explore new heights. Explore waterways, rooftops, and other crevices to duke it out with enemies and even find special items that can help you along the way.”

The press release also notes that there’ll be more opportunities for personalisation than in past titles, allowing you to “change your favorite Goddesses’ colors, attach fun accessories wherever you like, strengthen Processor Unit equipment found in dungeons that boost stats, and craft with the classic Disc Make that helps Goddesses achieve new abilities”.

There’s no specific date for when this title will deploy in the west outside of a vague 2027 window, but physical versions will be available for both PlayStation consoles in North America. (In Europe, only the PS5 version will be getting a boxed release.)

Do we have any NepNep fans in our ranks? I actually only ever played a little bit of the first one which was undoubtedly scruffy, but I know there’s a really strong following for this series which has kept it active for so long.

#4078. Ghost of Yotei studio Sucker Punch reportedly lays off 26 developers "after carefully observing the challenges in the market"

The PlayStation-owned developer is making cuts.

Layoffs have reportedly hit Sucker Punch, the PlayStation-owned studio behind the Sly Cooper series, Infamous and last year's Ghost of Yotei.

Aftermath reports that 26 workers have been affected by the cuts, citing a former employee. According to an email sent to staff and seen by Aftermath, studio leadership blamed layoffs on the shaky state of the industry and "the needs" of the developer's next, unannounced game.

"After carefully observing the challenges in the market and reviewing the team needs for our next project, we've decided to make some staffing reductions. Several positions across Sucker Punch will be eliminated as a result," studio higher ups wrote.

"We know this is a lot to take in, and we want to assure you that we did not make this decision lightly. We have given this a lot of attention and worked to support our affected colleagues during this transition as well as we can… There's no getting around that this is a hard day. Next week we will go into more details about the future."

Sucker Punch's last game, the gorgeous open-world sequel Ghost of Yotei, was seemingly a big hit for PlayStation. Ghost of Yotei sold 3.3m copies about a month after launch, outperforming other PS5 favourites such as Astro Bot in the same time period.

While Sony hasn't published updated financial figures since then, the console maker did say Ghost of Yotei "exceeded the sales of the previous title in the same period of time" when reporting its financials for the quarter ending on the 31st of December. Ghost of Tsushima sold upwards of 13m copies across consoles and PC, though Sony is seemingly done bringing its signature single-player games to PC. As ever in the games industry, even success can't protect talented developers from layoffs.

This summer's Ghost of Yotei: Complete Edition re-release came with an interesting roguelike mode, additional cosmetics, a story-focused bonus episode called Echoes of Sekigahara and much more.

#4077. Xbox Nano Controller Gets Its First Reviews, And A Secret Hidden Feature Is Revealed

Update [Wed 4th Nov 2026, 7:33pm]: That hidden feature is now public, with Xbox announcing it today:

News Xbox Announces Two New Methods To Play Games Through The Cloud

"Starting today, we’re rolling out two previews for XBOX Cloud Gaming."

Original Story: Today's the day for the Xbox Nano Controller! This mini design with a portable nature goes on sale for £44.99 / $49.99 with a release date of November 4th, and therefore the first reviews have started going live for it.

Before we get to those, we also want to bring your attention to a secret hidden feature of the Xbox Nano Controller that's been uncovered by The Verge, which is that it can connect directly to Xbox Cloud Gaming via Wi-Fi in order to reduce latency when playing over the cloud.

The outlet expects this to be announced soon by Microsoft (it's seemingly still in testing internally), and that it'll also likely be part of the Xbox Elite Series 3 Controller whenever it releases as well. Windows Central believes that the tech will be part of "all future Xbox controllers".

"I’m expecting Microsoft to announce this as a preview for the new Xbox Nano controller soon, before it’s fully supported across Xbox Cloud Gaming on the web and on smart TVs."

So, let's get to those reviews! Here's what the critics are saying about the Nano controller so far:

"The smallest Xbox-branded controller to date, the nano is designed for gamers with smaller hands. Its compact nature also means it’s easier to take it out and about with you. It’s basically a standard Xbox controller with all the controls you’d expect, but in a much smaller package. And for those reasons, it’s undoubtedly excellent. It’s easy to set up, doesn’t take up much room when you have it on you, and does exactly what it sets out to do. While this is not necessarily a bad thing, it doesn’t go hugely beyond that, though."

"I’m not young, but I do have small hands, and I’ve been surprised at how comfortable the Nano is during gaming sessions. At just over 5 inches long, almost everything on this controller has been shrunk down somehow. The ABXY buttons are ever so slightly smaller than a regular Xbox controller, and the thumbsticks feel like miniature versions. Microsoft hasn’t changed the D-pad, though, or the size of the glowing Xbox button at the center of the controller."

"I recommend the Nano for someone who likes to game on the go, travels frequently or has smaller hands. It’s not as diminutive as other similarly sized controllers, and that extra size makes the Nano more comfortable than those other mobile controllers — but when I’m home, I’ll stick with my full-size gamepads, thanks."

"In any case, this is a really nice addition to the Xbox controller lineup. It's going to be ideal for travel due to its weight and size, and is easily pocketable. It might also be a better option for younger gamers with smaller hands. Microsoft has been marketing it against Minecraft Dungeons 2, which offers a glimpse at how they're thinking about positioning it."

As you can see, the Nano Controller seems to be a nice addition for anyone who wants a really compact design built for portability and small hands, and it certainly won't break the bank at its price point.

We'll hopefully have our own review of the Nano here at Pure Xbox very soon, but we haven't got our hands on it just yet. Look out for our impressions later in November!

#4075. "We basically rewrote the entire State of Decay game": Undead Labs spent years trying to make State of Decay 3 into a full-blown zombie apocalypse MMO

State of Decay 3 was announced with a snazzy cinematic trailer all the way back in 2020. The open-world zombie game was due to move to colder climes, where you would face undead deer and survive the frigid elements. We've since learned that the teaser bore very little resemblance to what was actually being worked on, and was pushed out the door to plump up a Microsoft showcase.

However, what the teaser also didn't reveal was that Undead Labs' ideas for the game were much larger in scope than the two survival games that came before. For several years they were trying to make State of Decay 3 into an MMO that captured the scale of a global zombie apocalypse.

In an interview with GamesIndustry.biz detailing the recent move to independence after Xbox cut the studio loose, Undead Labs CEO Philip Holt explains that the team's founder, Jeff Strain, planned to expand the series from its co-op roots into a full MMO. While Strain left the studio in 2019, his ideas remained with the small team working on the prototypes for State of Decay 3. "He always had a vision of making an MMO and the ultimate global scale of a zombie apocalypse," Holt says. "And so there was just a different set of creative objectives the team was trying to pursue at that time."

After State of Decay 3 was announced in 2020, a small team worked on developing the technology to support an MMO, while the rest of the studio continued supporting State of Decay 2. However, towards the end of 2022, Holt and the team decided to go back to a game that better resembled the scale of the first two games. "There was a pretty significant pivot creatively on State of Decay 3's development," Holt tells GI. "So I would say the game that's present today has really been built probably since '23, maybe late '22." Later in the interview saying "One of the things I learned is just how much respect I have for teams that make successful MMOs, because I've seen them swallow people whole."

It wasn't a flippant change, as it meant throwing out much of what had already been made. "We basically rewrote the entire State of Decay game, and we will not do that again," Holt says. "We have the benefit now of this pretty significant investment in software that we got to figure out how to make the most of. We hope that State of Decay 3 has a long and successful life and becomes a live and evolving game. But yeah, I think it's highly unlikely that we spend as much time on the next game as we did on State of Decay 3."

Though, it did mean that when Xbox cut ties with Undead Labs they had a project near enough to release that they've been able to find a publisher willing to fund State of Decay 3's final months of development. Still, even with that support, Undead Labs still had to lay off "a significant number" of staff.

I've a real soft spot for the state of Decay games, though I've never played them in multiplayer. For me, they were always an apocalypse I could mooch around in solo, gradually expanding my survivors' camp and making a dent in the zombie hordes that roamed across the environment. An MMO take on the same world wouldn't have appealed to my misanthropic sensibilities, but I'm interested to learn how the tech that was produced has been rolled into the current version of State of Decay 3.

Still, one day, I want to face down a zombie deer. Granted, I'll immediately run and hide, but it'd be nice to see one.

#4074. Amid sweeping layoffs at Xbox and massive AI investments, Microsoft introduces a "Voluntary Exit Offer" to 60,000 workers

Xbox isn't the only Microsoft division looking to massively reduce worker headcounts. In fact, Microsoft has just announced a "Voluntary Exit Offer" that will essentially pay staff to move in front of any potential layoffs and voluntarily leave their jobs.

Microsoft CPO Amy Coleman announced the plan earlier today. "This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organizations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs," Colemon wrote in a memo sent to staff.

The voluntary buyout is only available to Microsoft employees "at level 70 and below" in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States. Some corners of the company have opted out of the offer - it's currently unclear if Xbox or any of the studios under its umbrella are participating in the initiative.

"This is a time-limited, voluntary program that gives those who are eligible the opportunity to leave Microsoft with financial support and career planning resources. Some organizations are providing the Voluntary Exit Offer, and some are not. Participation varies based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs," Coleman added.

A Microsoft spokesperson told Business Insider that the offer will be available to about 60,000 employees, roughly 25 percent of the company's total workforce - a staggering figure. According to the outlet, Microsoft's voluntary exit offer has similar terms to the company's severance packages, and eligible workers need to decide if they'll lay themselves off by early December.

Xbox embarked on a huge "reset" earlier this year, which involved a planned 3,200 jobs cuts and a massive internal restructure for many of its first-party studios. Double Fine, Compulsion Games and Undead Labs have all gone independent since then, while the fates of Arkane Lyon and Ninja Theory are still shaky. As CNBC noted, the voluntary buyout was announced as Microsoft tries to balance its sky-high spending in generative AI.

#4073. Hot Wax sets fire to the Tetris playbook with slow-burn puzzle mechanics and a dollop of eldritch menace

Over the past couple of weeks, I've been conscious of an eerie background humming and hissing. For a while I thought it was just tinnitus, brought on by one too many listens of Control's Ashtray Maze OST, but then I realised that it was actually RPS regular quasiotter whispering in my ear about Hot Wax, which launches on Steam this week after a spell of Itch.io exclusivity.

It's the new arcade puzzler from PUNKCAKE Délicieux, otherwise known for inflicting shotguns on chess and forcing the alphabet to wear trousers in the name of archaeology, somehow. Hot Wax is actually quite straightforward by PUNKCAKE standards. It's Tetris, but all the blocks are candles, and rather than filling a line on the grid to clear blocks, you have to plant unpredictably dropped flames on wicks to slowly sizzle the mass away. Relatively straightforward, yes, but fiddly in practice. Did I mention that you're doing all this in a temple, under the eye of a "not unfriendly" eldritch god?

There's still a demo for Hot Wax on Steam, with the full release due in Valve's cathedral of commerce tomorrow. I've had a go at that demo, and it has tickled my brain. You need to line up candles, wick to wick, rather than just filling gaps, as in Tetris. But you still, ideally, need to avoid gaps to slow down the filling of the screen. Once a wick is lit, it'll gradually melt the candle and leap to any other wicks it touches.

Once a candle is lit, you have to avoid smothering it by unscientifically dunking another candle on top of it, while trying to take advantage of how the melting wax alters the layout. I found this enjoyably challenging. And then there are the power-up items, acquired by sacrificing flames to the aforesaid "not unfriendly" god. These include bombs that light a bunch of wicks at once, and acorns that sprout a column-filling sapling. Not sure what they worship in this temple, exactly, other than Tetris.

There will be a bunch of modes in the full release – from basic score attack and endless play, to a mode where you have to melt several, painstakingly arranged candles with just one flame. They're also planning daily seeded challenge runs. As with PUNKCAKE stuff at large, it's a looker, with some lustrous pixel art and lots of nifty little animations. Thank you, quasiotter – this was fun! You can stop going "EEEEEEEE" in my ear now.

#4071. Modern Warfare 4 Boosts Call Of Duty Players On Xbox, But Falls Short Of Black Ops 7 Impact

We heard plenty of noise when Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 launched, earning the highest review scores the series has seen since Black Ops on Xbox 360. Now, Circana's Mat Piscatella has shared some new data showing just how well the game performed during its opening week.

Cricana ranks games based on its weekly player counts (not concurrent players), and places them into a top 10 list. Call of Duty shot up the standings following the release of Modern Warfare 4 (W/E October 24), ranking highly across PlayStation (PS4 and PS5) and Xbox's worldwide player standings.

Circana Player Engagement Tracker - Top 10 Titles by Weekly Active Users (Not Concurrent) - W/E Oct 24, 2026 - Call of Duty lifted across ecosystems with MW4 launch, including jumping from 32nd to 6th on US Steam - Cyberpunk 2077 returned to top 20 across ecosystems with Edgerunners 2 Update

As you can see above, COD climbed two places to take 2nd spot on Sony hardware. Whereas, on Xbox, the shooter leapfrogged NBA 2K27 to claim the bronze. It's biggest jump in weekly active players came on Steam's US charts, where Call of Duty rocketed from 32nd to 6th.

It's no surprise that Modern Warfare 4's release gave COD's active player numbers a significant boost, however, when compared with the impact of Black Ops 7's launch in 2025, the numbers aren't quite as positive.

Circana Player Engagement Tracker % of Active Panel playing Call of Duty: Week Ending Oct 24th, 2026 (Modern Warfare 4 Launch): US PS - 19% WW XBX - 17% US Steam - 4.2% Week Ending Nov 15th, 2025 (Black Ops 7 Launch): US PS - 23% WW XBX - 29% US Steam - 1.5%

On Xbox, Call of Duty accounted for 17% of active players during the week of MW4's launch, compared with 29% during Black Ops 7's 2025 launch. Of course, BO7 had a much larger player pool to draw from, having launched as the last Call of Duty day one title on Xbox Game Pass. On top of that, Modern Warfare 4 had a staggered launch, offering early access to its campaign and DMZ modes ahead of the full release on October 23rd.

#4070. Mass Effect fans ramp up efforts to save BioWare's RPG series with a Times Square billboard and plans for more ads outside The Game Awards

Fans continue to rally around the 'Save Mass Effect' movement, this time with a billboard at Times Square and more initiatives planned throughout the rest of the year.

Last week, publisher EA shut down BioWare and cancelled the next Mass Effect game. In the days since, an increasingly loud community-organised campaign has attempted to make Electronic Arts reverse course and ensure that the beloved sci-fi universe can journey forward in some form.

🚨 WE'RE IN TIMES SQUARE! Together with @kalaelizabeth, we've managed to get a #SaveMassEffect billboard up in Times Square, NYC, all day today! 📍 1560 Broadway, above the Pelé store (Duffy Square) ⏰ 15 seconds every hour at :35 HOLD THE LINE! ❤️ https://t.co/wNP9Ak9Vh8

The We Are Mass Effect community group and content creator Kala Elizabeth are now collaborating on a number of initiatives, including a billboard at New York City's Times Square that points people toward the growing online "SaveMassEffect" hashtag. Text that reads "Kellah Si'yah" is sprawled across the ad - referencing the in-game ship that ferried different races to settle the Andromeda system.

"Apart from the Times Square billboard, we also have several other initiatives in the works. An advertising truck near EA's headquarters in Redwood City and in Edmonton, a mobile billboard for N7 Day, and another one in LA for The Game Awards. All of them will carry a message in support of #SaveMassEffect," one of the group's organisers, Mer Mora, told me via email.

The 'SaveMassEffect' petition gained a huge amount of traction this weekend with 226,000 signatures and counting. The petition urges rights holder EA to commit to "the continued development of Mass Effect" by either funding a new game in the series or by licensing it to an outside studio who can do it justice.

"All of these initiatives will be funded by the community itself! We're putting together a GoFundMe after receiving an overwhelming response from community members eager to contribute financially to make all of these happen," Mora added. "And given the incredible support and generosity we've received, any funds raised beyond our goal will be donated to the Game Workers' Hardship Fund, which supports game developers who have been laid off." The United Videogame Workers union (UVW-CWA) opened the fund earlier this year to support the many laid off video game workers across Canada and the USA.

#4068. Subnautica 2 dev thinks early access teams should worry less about adding features that are "very ugly, incomplete, or prototype"

But acknowledges that "early access" ain't what it was

Subnautica 2 creative director Anthony Gallegos has spoken about what Unknown Worlds have learned over their many years working in Steam early access, exhorting other devs to add new features "as soon as possible" and experiment with them right under the flared nostrils of players. Damn the torpedoes, etcetera.

The original Subnautica is one of the oldest Steam early access success stories, launching in 2014 a month or so after the program went live. Many of the final version's better qualities, including the pivot to horror epitomised by the spectacle of a Reaper grabbing your submarine's face, reflect observation of players and streamers in the wilds.

"Subnautica often launched features when they were very ugly, incomplete, or prototype," Gallegos commented, as part of a group chat about early access with GamesIndustry.biz. "This gave fans a real sense of getting to see game development in progress, in a way few other studios would try, especially for a franchise as big as this."

Unknown Worlds have "cultivated a very empathetic audience through radical transparency," Gallegos continued. "We trust the audience to give us a little grace as we figure things out, and they in turn trust us to make it great in the fullness of time."

Naturally, Gallegos thinks it's vital to keep talking to players and taking their feedback on the chin. "Be honest with them and make them understand how crucial they are to the process," he went on. "Preserve your vision, but listen to them and let them help you bring the best out of your game." Early access remains "core" to the "DNA" of Unknown Worlds, as they continue with the creation of Subnautica 2, which is about to get a nourishing injection of robot frogs.

I'm writing this up mostly because I'd like to know where you all stand as regards the "very ugly, incomplete, or prototype" - which, now that I think about it, sounds like the film Sergio Leone might have made, if he'd gotten into industry documentaries rather than spaghetti westerns. My view on early access is basically that it has become the same things as live service. I'm not sure there's a meaningful division any more between labelling a game "unfinished" and the expectation that devs will keep adding stuff to any release.

Within that, though, there's a lot of diversity, as Gallegos acknowledges in the GI piece. "Early access could mean a game like ours doing long-term open development, or it could be a game three months from a 1.0 release that's effectively doing a paid beta soft launch and using the Early Access term as a way to soften player expectations," he observed.

Not everybody has been as fortunate as Unknown Worlds in persuading players to give them the benefit of the doubt. In a crowded market (GI say that 2,924 early access games have launched on Steam this year so far, citing SteamDB), newer teams may suffer from being compared to older operators like Unknown Worlds, who got involved when early access was still fresh and exotic.

Elsewhere in the GI article, Denis Dyack, CEO of Deadhaus Sonata developer Apocalypse Studios, argues that expectations are unavoidably set by the early access devs with the largest budgets, citing Subnautica 2 as an example.

Back to you, the atrocious buyer of unfinshed games: what do you expect from an early access release? What degree of wobble will you overlook? What are you happy for devs to leave out till the final version? How important is communication, really? Does it just depend totally on the game? Here is some topical music to think along to.

#4067. Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced's final major update adds long-awaited New Game Plus, new Nightmare difficulty and much more

After a period of quiet and a few small updates, Ubisoft has unveiled a massive update coming today to Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced. This is the game's last major patch and it includes some long-requested features.

Update 1.0.8 goes live on PC, PS5 and Xbox Series X/S today (27th October) at 7am PT, 10am ET, 2pm UK. It's a relatively small download on all platforms - between 2 and 4.5GB - except Xbox, where it's a whopping 15.5GB.

The new update's biggest addition is New Game Plus mode, which Ubisoft started working on in July after releasing Resynced. Much of what's earned and unlocked in your current playthrough carries over to NG+, but not everything does. Here's what carries over:

While cash and trade goods do carry over, quest-related items do not. Forts also need to be re-taken, as NG+ resets the map's fog of war.

The NG+ mode has a new exclusive currency - Escudos - earned by completing challenges and looting previously unlocked chests. The currency can be spent on NG+ exclusive outfits and items, and you'll be able to exchange Reales for Escudos at the General Store, too.

Naturally, the game difficulty increases with each NG+ run. Elite soldiers, for instance, will appear more often, and max rank ships will be a more common sight across the water. You can enter NG+ up to five times, with each further runthrough increasing the challenge.

Patch 1.0.8 also introduces Nightmare Mode, a new brutal difficulty setting. Ubisoft said enemy reaction times and the damage they deal are ramped up. Parry timings are tighter, and ranged enemies will target you more often.

What may be the biggest change, however, is the removal of the one-shot kill safety. In other words, the game won't prevent you from receiving instant deaths, such as in cases where you take high burst damage from bullets and explosives. In those cases, you're going to die, even if you have HP left. The goal was to create a harsh experience "where every duel can be your last".

Elsewhere in the patch, there are new community chests hidden around the game's world for players to uncover. There's a set of new cosmetics, new takedown animations, and, of course, a litany of bug fixes. The full change log is on the official Assassin's Creed website. It's worth reading if you're looking to attempt a playthrough on Nightmare to see what it changes.

Though that may be Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced's last big update, the game is seemingly on its way to Switch 2, and that version should include all previously-released additions, as we've come to expect.

#4066. Mini Review: Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered (PS5) - Nostalgic Kaiju Brawls in This Fun But Meagre Package

Godzilla is approaching the generator, the generator is losing power

Version Reviewed: PS5 (Standard) / European

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee was a grand arena brawler in its day, especially if you consider yourself a fan of the king of the monsters. With a fun roster of characters, an impressive array of arenas, and solid gameplay, the title was a kaiju fan's dream.

That sentiment is still true with this remaster. Outside of a couple of small tweaks, the core gameplay that was such a success nearly 25 years ago is still intact.

Controlling Godzilla or any number of the other creatures from the big green lizard's rogues gallery is a blast, though you only get four characters to choose from at the start.

Gigan is especially fun, with light, nimble attacks. Some of the best kaiju are sadly absent, like Biollante. Hedorah was formerly present, but has been removed for the remaster, though mercifully Mothra remains.

Getting into a flow state with timing your attacks and watching large creatures go flying across a cityscape is immensely satisfying. The sound design is weighty — and authentic to the movies, featuring many iconic sound effects — and the wanton destruction the monsters leave in their wake has never looked better.

In fact, the game looks brilliant on all fronts. All the updates to the game's visuals are most welcome. Textures are crisp, environments pop, and the frame rate is rock solid.

The most notable change from the original probably comes by way of the unlock system, which, while not egregious, has been turned into a bit of a "games as a service" grind, though most everything is easy to get just from playing the game.

Whether or not yo'’ll stick around to unlock everything is another story, however. While the game is great fun, it's not terribly deep. The "story" mode can be run through in about 15 minutes if you take your time, and the other modes offer only fleeting enjoyment. Survival sees you fighting kaiju until you lose, and Destruction simply has you destroy buildings for a high score. There's just not enough substance here to keep you coming back in the long term.

The remaster ends up offering a brief jolt of fun, and while it may not keep you coming back to play it, the little time that you do spend with it will be memorable and enjoyable. And if you consider yourself a Godzilla fan, this is ultimately still a must-play.

#4065. "We are more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly": Epic get more specific about genAI use in Unreal Engine and Fortnite development

Epic Games are, dunno if you've heard, on a bit of a genAI kick at the moment. It's been tough to notice unless you listen very hard. Tim Sweeney's lips have been sealed and no reports have spewed forth.

Sark aside, to this point Epic have had far more provocative soundbites and weird marketing lingo to offer than specific detail about how they're using genAI in different parts of their business.

Responding to questioning from This Week in Videogames, Epic's executive vice president of development Marcus Wassmer's run through some of the exact tools and uses that make up the company's current deployment of the tech.

"There are a number of tools in use but probably the most obvious ones are Claude Code and Codex with their associated AI models," he said "They’re helping across a broad spectrum of development, with some particularly big recent wins being almost the complete elimination of non-deterministic cooking bugs which we’ve been fighting for a decade and an acceleration of work related to compressing shaders which both significantly reduce patch sizes. [Other wins include] a rewrite of a significant portion of the D3D12 rendering layer (which I estimated as needing three to six weeks of work for a single engineer, but the work was actually completed in about one week with a nice win on CPU time and fewer bugs), lots of help in keeping our internal test suites healthy as well as expanding those test suites for more coverage."

Wassmer went on to add that Fortnite's seen the additions of "automatic monitoring of PC stability", "automatic root cause analysis and automatic fix generation", which he claims have sped up the rectifying of long-running issues. He also noted that, engine-wise, Epic have been able to attempt "some larger architectural refactors with AI" than they previously could due to the amount of file changes required.

The dev went on to confirm that the Epic Store launcher preview released the other week isn't the only bit of vibe-coding the company have been up to, with the practice also being used in Unreal Engine development. "Yes, we are vibe-coding things," he said. "That means our engineers are no longer writing the bulk of the code, but they are still guiding the tools to get the architectural result we want. We’re not ‘one-shotting’ the engine; we’re iterating with AI to ship features developers want and keep the engine within the memory, performance, and scalability envelopes."

Wassmer also managed to fit in some justification as to why Epic see no other way forward then shoving a bunch of genAI into their development, largely parroting the typical talking point of 'everyone's going to be doing it soon and we can't possibly be seen to miss out on that gold rush for short-term speediness, baby'. "We are more concerned about the risks of moving too slowly than we are about AI skepticism," is one of the lines he actually said.

To be fair, at least Wassmer and Epic aren't hiding the fact they're embracing this stuff, as much as Timmy Sweens hates the concept of devs having to disclose their genAI use to prospective customers or users. Sometimes the desire of AI bros to shout about their use from the rooftops out of sheer marketing zeal has its positives, eh?

#4064. Composer shares 20 minutes of music created for Mass Effect 5 following tragic closure of BioWare

Austin Wintory has shared twenty minutes of music they pitched to BioWare and EA in hopes of joining the Mass Effect 5 development team, following the tragic closure of BioWare last week.

The composer, known for his work on Journey and Sword of the Sea, uploaded the music to his personal YouTube channel. It was made without knowledge of the narrative direction of the new Mass Effect game, but was presented as a surprise to the companies in 2025 as part of years of conversation. Wintory writes in the video that it was a "direct homage" to Mass Effect 1 composers Jack Wall and Sam Hulick, leaning into analog synths and "a more complex integration of the orchestra", a hybrid approach Wintory compares to The Matrix movies scores.

This collection of music includes a track called The Legacy of Shepard, which includes "deliberate winks" to the original Mass Effect theme. The second track - Sailing the Relays - features the blend of synth and orchestra mentioned earlier quite heavily. All in all, there are eight tracks included in total, with the eighth being a remix of that first Legacy of Shepard composition.

The video's description contains a sombre message on BioWare's closure, as well as gratitude towards the music departments involved in the conversations Wintory took part it: "Receiving the news alongside everyone else that EA had decided to not only cancel the project but shutdown BioWare entirely was a deeply felt loss. It's been hard to see dear friends lose their jobs, and this beloved franchise seemingly vanish forever.

"Thank you nonetheless to everyone at BioWare and EA's music department for gifting me the chance to dream in your sandbox. It was a privilege to do even that much."

Wintory is not alone in their sadness. EA's closure of BioWare, which included the firing of 50 employees and a further 350 across other EA-owned studios, many across the industry came forward to decry the decision. The decision may even have political ramifications, as one Canadian party leader has expressed a desire to allow BioWare employees to buy back the studio with federal support. This all happened shortly after EA's $55bn private acquisition from Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner and Saudi Arabia's Savvy Games Group.

#4062. Nintendo's Inventory Levels At A Record High As RAM Crisis Continues

As part of its latest financial report, Nintendo has published the yen value of its inventory for the second quarter of FY2026/27, showing a record high as the company attempts to mitigate rising costs across the industry.

The latest quarterly report states that the platform holder has 814.57 billion yen's worth (approximately £3.8 billion / $5.14 billion) of inventory in its warehouses as of 30th September. That's an increase from 539.8 billion yen the previous quarter.

As highlighted by Nintendo Patents Watch, this is a new record for the firm as manufacturers across tech sectors navigate the global RAM shortage and attempt to avoid — or at least delay — further price increases.

Another quarter, another new record of inventory level. In just three months, Nintendo increased the inventories by ¥197B to a total of ¥815B (~US$5.15B). This is an astronomical number for a video game company, but is necessary to hedge against rising memory costs.

Nintendo raised the cost of Switch 2 worldwide earlier this year, following in the footsteps of Sony and Microsoft, who have hiked hardware prices multiple times in recent years.

It's a tough time for the industry, with recent reports suggesting that Microsoft's next Xbox could cost as much as $1800. The massive costs of developing and manufacturing systems and sourcing the necessary memory and components arguably put Nintendo in a better position than the competition in the short term, as both PS5 and Xbox Series X|S launched in 2020 compared to 2025 for Switch 2.

Nintendo managed to build a substantial inventory of Switch 2 units prior to launch and will want to have as many units as possible available ahead of the holidays following today's launch of Zelda: Ocarina of Time and the recent Zelda 40th Anniversary Switch 2.

It is worth noting that Nintendo's research and development costs rose 16.8% to 96.2 billion yen this quarter. This lends credence to rumours that the firm may be developing a 'Switch 2 Lite' or other hardware, although we wouldn't expect to see any revised hardware announcements anytime soon.

For comparison, Switch Lite arrived in 2019, two-and-a-half years after the launch of Switch 1. Assuming a similar timescale, Holiday 2027 could be the target launch window for a hypothetical Switch 2 Lite, but given the industry climate and challenges — not to mention the wider economy — that feels ambitious.

#4061. Company of Heroes 3's Operation Torch DLC ships off to North Africa in November, for new missions based around the Allied landings

Atten-shun! Company Of Heroes 3's got new single-player missions inbound via a DLC set during the Allies' 1942 invasion of North Africa. You'll take charge of American forces through a campaign steeped in second world war history that's designed to test your tactical nous and ability to upgrade fighting units to come out on top.It's out on November 25th.

As is made rather obvious by its name, the DLC depicts Operation Torch, which saw the Brits and yanks work together to invade Vichy France-controlled Algeria and Morocco. There's a "dramatic campaign arc that spans the opening invasion, the defeat at Kasserine, and the final assault on Hill 609", no doubt with copious mentions of names like Eisenhower and Patton across its 15 missions.

You'll don the boots of three American soldiers who're either in command or in the thick of the action on the battlefield, with devs Relic noting that their "perspectives reflect the hardships, losses, responsibilities, and lessons learned as they are forged into the fighting force that will liberate Europe".

In between the likes of urban tank battles and stealth ops, you'll pick upgrades earned through completing objectives, ensuring your troops fight in the manner that best suits your preferred tactical slant. For example, I assume you'll be able to go all-in on artillery if all you're after is some big booms that look impressive, but might prove useless if the enemy are safely tucked away in deep cover waving their middle fingers at your boys.

"Company Of Heroes 3 is a rip-roaring return to form and then some for Relic's much loved RTS, and its stirring orchestral score will have you beating your chest and yelling hoo-rah like only the best toy soldier fantasies can," former RPS commander-in-chief Katharine wrote of COH 3 on release in 2023. "If Relic can iron out some of those lingering campaign niggles, this could easily be an all-timer for WWII strategy buffs."

More recently, current boss Julian gave roguelite spin-off Company of Heroes 3: Final Stand a go, coming out with the impression that it's a shakeup which succeded in increasing his appreciation for the series.
